description: Data vs information, the five data types, and how validation and verification tools reduce user errors.
hero_image_caption: A data entry form on screen showing fields with different data types and input controls.
content_html:
Data and Information — Not the Same Thing

Students often use the words “data” and “information” as if they mean the same thing. They do not. Data is raw, unprocessed facts — numbers, letters or symbols that mean nothing without context. Information is data that has been processed and given meaning.

The key step is processing. Take the raw numbers 17, 19 and 22: on their own they are meaningless data. Process them — calculate the average, attach labels and a date — and you get the useful statement: “The average daily temperature in Manchester this week was 19°C.” This distinction matters on the exam: an answer that simply says the numbers are “information” without describing the processing step will lose a mark.

Key Fact

Data is raw, unprocessed facts (e.g. “17, 19, 22”). Information is data that has been processed and given context to make it meaningful. Processing is the step that converts one into the other.

Data Types

Choosing the correct data type is essential when designing any IT system. The five main data types are alphanumeric, Boolean, date, numeric and text. Each has specific characteristics that make it suitable for different kinds of data.

Alphanumeric combines letters and numbers — ideal for postcodes (SW1A 1AA), reference numbers (INV-2024-001) and registration plates. Boolean stores only two values: true or false (or yes/no, 1/0). It suits any yes/no field, such as whether a customer has agreed to marketing emails. Date stores date values in a consistent format (e.g. DD/MM/YYYY) and allows date-based calculations such as working out how many days until an order is due.

Text stores any string of characters without treating them as numbers — used for names, addresses and descriptions where calculation is not needed. Numeric covers several sub-types: integer (whole numbers, e.g. quantity in stock), real or decimal (numbers with a decimal point, e.g. 4.99), currency (formatted decimal, e.g. £4.99), and percentage (a decimal expressed as a percentage, e.g. 12.5%).

Validation is an automated check that data is reasonable and in the right format. It happens automatically as the user types or submits a form. For example, a validation rule might check that an age field contains a number between 0 and 120.

Crucially, validation cannot check whether data is true. If someone enters their age as 25 when they are actually 30, the validation rule accepts the value — it is a plausible number. Validation only catches data that is impossible or implausible.

Verification checks that data has been entered correctly by comparing it against the original source. The two verification methods are double entry (asking the user to type the same data twice, e.g. confirming a password) and manual checking (a person compares printed output against the original document). Verification catches transcription errors that validation cannot detect.

Data Validation Tools

There are nine named validation tools. A data type check ensures the entry matches the expected data type (e.g. rejects letters in a numeric field). A format check tests that data follows a specific pattern — for example, an input mask for a UK postcode allows only the pattern AA99 9AA. A length check ensures the entry is not too short or too long (e.g. a PIN must be exactly 4 digits).

A limited choice tool restricts the user to a predefined set of values. This includes drop-down lists (the user selects from a visible list), radio buttons (the user selects one option from a small set) and tick lists (the user checks one or more boxes). A lookup checks that the entry exists in a reference table — for example, checking that a customer ID exists in the customer database before an order is placed. A presence check ensures a required field is not left blank. A range check ensures a numeric value falls within acceptable limits (e.g. exam scores must be between 0 and 100).

Exam questions often give a scenario (e.g. a hospital booking system) and ask you to justify a data type or validation tool for a specific field. Work through the field’s purpose: does it store numbers used in calculations? Use a numeric type. Does it need a specific pattern? Use a format check or input mask. Is it a yes/no field? Use Boolean. Must it come from a fixed list? Use a drop-down list or radio buttons.

Remember: validation is automatic (built into the form), verification is a human or repeated-entry check. A hospital patient’s date of birth field would use a date data type, a format check to enforce DD/MM/YYYY, a range check to ensure it is not in the future, and might use double entry (verification) to confirm the nurse typed it correctly.

Key Fact

The nine validation tools are: data type check, format check, input mask, length check, limited choice (drop-down list / radio buttons / tick list), lookup, presence check and range check. These can appear in any exam scenario question.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on data/validation questions is confusing validation and verification. Use this quick test: validation is automated and checks whether data is reasonable; verification checks whether data was entered correctly (by double entry or manual checking). If a question uses the command word “explain”, you must include a connecting phrase such as “because” or “this means that” — listing two validation tools without explaining what each one does will only score partial marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Data is raw unprocessed facts; information is data that has been processed and given context. The processing step is what converts one into the other.
  • The five data types are alphanumeric, Boolean, date, numeric (integer, real, decimal, currency, percentage) and text — each suits specific kinds of stored values.
  • Validation is an automated check that data is reasonable (nine named tools); verification checks data was entered correctly via double entry or manual checking. They serve different purposes and both reduce errors.

practice_questions.text: Which data type stores only two possible values: true or false?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Boolean (only). Distractors: text (stores any characters), alphanumeric (letters and numbers), integer (whole numbers).

practice_questions.text: Identify the validation tool that checks a required field has not been left empty.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: presence check (only). Do not accept range check (tests numeric limits) or data type check (tests format).

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between data and information.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: data is raw, unprocessed facts with no context (1); information is data that has been processed and given meaning (1). Award 1 mark if only one side is described. Do not award marks for treating them as synonyms.

practice_questions.text: Describe how an input mask is used as a data validation tool. Use an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: an input mask enforces a specific pattern for data entry (1), for example, restricting a postcode field to the pattern of two letters, two numbers, a space, a number and two letters — so 'SW1A 1AA' would be accepted but '1234' would be rejected (1). Award 1 mark for an accurate description without an example.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a hospital appointment system would use double-entry verification for a patient's date of birth, rather than relying on validation alone.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): validation checks that the date is in the correct format and is not in the future (1), but it cannot check whether the date entered is actually the correct date for that patient (1), so double-entry verification requires the receptionist to type the date of birth a second time, catching transcription errors before they are saved (1).
Secure (2): identifies that validation and verification serve different purposes with one clear explanation.
Developing (1): states that double entry is 'more accurate' without explaining why or what each method checks.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe four data types that could be used in a system that stores customer orders for an online clothing shop. For each, name a specific field it would apply to.
practice_questions.marks: 4 marks, 1 per accurate data type + field pairing. Accept any four from: text — customer name (names contain no calculated values) (1); integer — quantity of items ordered (whole number, no decimal needed) (1); currency/decimal — price per item (needs decimal point and currency symbol) (1); date — delivery date (stored in DD/MM/YYYY format for date calculations) (1); Boolean — gift wrap required (yes/no field) (1); alphanumeric — product code (combination of letters and numbers such as SHIRT-BLU-M) (1). Accept other valid pairings with clear justification.

knowledge_checks.q: A field that stores a product code such as 'CHAIR-RED-L' would use which data type?
Which verification method asks the user to type the same data twice to confirm it is correct?
A _____ check ensures that a numeric value falls within an acceptable range, such as exam scores between 0 and 100.
Data becomes _____ once it has been processed and given context to make it meaningful.
Match each data type to an appropriate field.
right: Delivery date stored in DD/MM/YYYY format
Whether a customer has agreed to marketing (yes/no)

flashcard_questions.a: Data is raw unprocessed facts; information is data processed and given context.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an alphanumeric data type?
flashcard_questions.a: A combination of letters and numbers, used for postcodes or product codes.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a Boolean data type store?
flashcard_questions.a: Only two values: true or false (yes/no).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a presence check?
flashcard_questions.a: Ensures a required field is not left blank.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a range check?
flashcard_questions.a: Ensures a numeric value falls within acceptable limits.
A validation tool that forces entry to follow a specific character pattern.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between validation and verification?
flashcard_questions.a: Validation checks data is reasonable (automated); verification checks it was entered correctly.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a lookup validation check?
flashcard_questions.a: That the entered value exists in a reference table.
Drop-down list, radio buttons, tick list.

glossary_terms.definition: Raw, unprocessed facts or figures that have no context on their own, such as the numbers 17, 19 and 22.
Data that has been processed and given context so that it is meaningful, such as the statement: the average daily temperature this week is 19 degrees.
A data type consisting of a combination of letters and numbers, used for fields such as postcodes or product codes.
An automated check that data entered into a system is reasonable, in the correct format or within expected limits — it cannot check whether the data is factually correct.
A check that confirms data has been entered correctly by comparing two entries or having a person check the original source — used to catch transcription errors.
A validation tool that forces data entry into a set pattern by only allowing certain characters in each position, such as LL99 9LL for a UK postcode.
